content: Shivering is a physiological response observed in warm-blooded animals when the body begins to experience early hypothermia. This reflex is initiated when the core body temperature drops below its normal range. In response, muscle groups surrounding vital organs engage in rapid, small-scale contractions. These movements are designed to generate heat through the expenditure of energy, thereby counteracting the drop in temperature. Shivering can also occur as a reaction to fever. In such cases, an individual may perceive a sensation of cold despite their core body temperature being elevated. This paradoxical response is due to the body's attempt to adjust to the altered thermoregulatory set point caused by the fever. The primary motor center responsible for shivering is located in the dorsomedial region of the hypothalamus, adjacent to the wall of the third ventricle. Under normal conditions, this center is inhibited by signals originating from the heat center in the anterior hypothalamic-preoptic area. However, it becomes activated when it receives cold signals from sensory inputs in the skin and spinal cord. Even a slight decrease in body temperature below a critical threshold can excite this center, triggering the shivering response.
